overview.title: Deploying a model as a REST API: export() to SavedModel and ONNX
overview.chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning
overview.main_topic: Serving a model behind a REST API using TensorFlow Serving or ONNX through Keras's export() method, and the conditions under which this setup is appropriate.
overview.central_idea: The easiest way to productize a model is to serve it online via a REST API. Keras supports TensorFlow Serving and ONNX out of the box through model.export(); both lift the weights and the computation graph out of Python, much like the compilation mechanism of chapter 3, so the model can be served from other environments such as a C++ server. Use this setup when the client has reliable internet, latency requirements are loose (about 500 ms round trip), and the input data is not highly sensitive.
overview.importance: This is the first and most common deployment option in the book's survey, and it shows the concrete Keras 3 API (export with format="tf_saved_model" or "onnx") for producing a Python-independent inference artifact.
learning_objectives: Explain what TensorFlow Serving and ONNX do: export weights plus a computation graph outside Python.
Relate exporting to the tf.function graph compilation from chapter 3.
Use model.export() for both formats and reload the artifacts for inference.
List the three conditions under which REST API deployment is appropriate.
prerequisites: Why models are exported for inference (p.208)

summary:
**Deploying a model as a REST API** is perhaps the easiest way to turn a model into a product. Among the many libraries for this, Keras supports two popular ones out of the box: **TensorFlow Serving** and **ONNX** (Open Neural Network Exchange). Both work by **lifting all model weights and a computation graph out of the Python program**, so the model can be served from other environments, for example a C++ server. This is essentially the **compilation mechanism of chapter 3**: TensorFlow Serving is a library for serving `tf.function` computation graphs with a specific set of saved weights.

Both are reachable through the **`export()`** method available on every Keras model. For TensorFlow Serving:

```python
model.export("path/to/location", format="tf_saved_model")
reloaded_artifact = tf.saved_model.load("path/to/location")
predictions = reloaded_artifact.serve(input_data)
```

The first line exports a TensorFlow SavedModel artifact; the reload lines can run in a different process, environment or programming language. ONNX follows the same flow with `format="onnx"`, then `onnxruntime.InferenceSession(...)` and `ort_session.run(None, input_data)`.

Use REST API deployment when:

- the consuming application has **reliable internet access**. A mobile app served from a remote API will not work in airplane mode or with poor connectivity;
- there are **no strict latency requirements**: request, inference and answer typically take **around 500 ms** round trip;
- the input data is **not highly sensitive**, because it must be available decrypted on the server for the model to see it (still use SSL encryption for the HTTP request and answer).

The next page lists example projects that fit this setup and discusses self-hosting versus managed cloud services, then turns to on-device deployment.

paragraphs.excerpt: Perhaps the easiest way to turn a model into a product is to
paragraphs.what_it_says: Serving a model online via a REST API is perhaps the easiest way to productize it. Keras supports TensorFlow Serving and ONNX out of the box. Both lift all model weights and a computation graph out of the Python program, so the model can be served from various environments such as a C++ server. This resembles the compilation mechanism from chapter 3: TensorFlow Serving essentially serves tf.function computation graphs with a specific set of saved weights.
paragraphs.what_it_means: In a REST setup, the client sends input data in an HTTP request to a server and receives predictions back. The model lives only on the server. To make that server fast and language-independent, you do not ship Python code; you ship a static description of the computation (the graph traced from the model's forward pass) plus the trained weights. That is what tracing a function with `tf.function` produced in chapter 3, now saved to disk.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It connects deployment to something you already understand: a compiled graph is a self-contained program that does not need the Python code that created it.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: ONNX is an open, framework-neutral graph format with operator definitions that many runtimes (ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, OpenVINO, ONNX Runtime Web) can execute, so it is a natural bridge across hardware and languages. A SavedModel is TensorFlow's on-disk format containing serialized graphs (signatures) and variable values.

concepts.name: REST API deployment
concepts.definition: Serving a model on a server that receives inputs over HTTP and returns predictions.
concepts.intuition: The model lives in a data center; clients phone in their questions.
concepts.technical: Uses an exported, Python-independent artifact (SavedModel served by TensorFlow Serving, or ONNX) on the server; round trip about 500 ms.
concepts.significance: Probably the easiest way to turn a model into a product.
concepts.example: A fraud-scoring service called by a payment backend.
concepts.misconception: That it suits every application; it fails without connectivity, under strict latency limits, or with highly sensitive inputs.

concepts.name: Model export (SavedModel, ONNX)
concepts.definition: Writing a model's weights and computation graph outside the Python program so other runtimes can execute it.
concepts.intuition: Freeze-drying the model: it no longer needs the kitchen it was cooked in.
concepts.technical: `model.export(path, format="tf_saved_model")` or `format="onnx"`; reload with `tf.saved_model.load(...).serve(x)` or `onnxruntime.InferenceSession(path).run(None, x)`.
concepts.significance: Makes deployment possible in non-Python environments such as C++ servers.
concepts.example: Training a Keras model with the JAX backend and serving its SavedModel export with TensorFlow Serving.
concepts.misconception: That an exported artifact can keep training like the original model; it is an inference artifact.

concepts.name: Computation graph (compilation)
concepts.definition: A static, traced representation of a function's tensor operations, executable without the original Python code.
concepts.intuition: A recorded recipe instead of a cook improvising each time.
concepts.technical: `tf.function` traces Python into a graph (chapter 3); TensorFlow Serving serves such graphs with saved weights.
concepts.significance: The mechanism that makes export and fast serving possible.
concepts.example: The graph of `relu(dot(x, W) + b)` operations plus the values of W and b.
concepts.misconception: That serving requires running your Python model class on the server.

code.title: Exporting and reloading a model for TensorFlow Serving
code.original_code:
model.export("path/to/location", format="tf_saved_model")

reloaded_artifact = tf.saved_model.load("path/to/location")
predictions = reloaded_artifact.serve(input_data)
code.what_it_does: Exports a Keras model as a TensorFlow SavedModel, then reloads that artifact and runs inference through its serve endpoint. Printed callouts: "Exports the model as a TensorFlow SavedModel artifact" (line 1) and "[Re]ads the artifact in a different process, environment, or programming language" (reload lines).

line_explanations.explanation: Writes the computation graph and weights to the directory in SavedModel format, the format TensorFlow Serving consumes.

Loads the artifact with TensorFlow's low-level loader. No Keras model class or training code is needed; this can happen in another process, environment, or (with TensorFlow's other-language APIs or TensorFlow Serving) another language.
Calls the exported `serve` endpoint (the inference function) on `input_data` to get predictions.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: a trained Keras model and an input batch `input_data` shaped like the model's inputs. Output: a SavedModel directory on disk and the prediction tensor.
code.algorithm: Trace the forward pass into a graph, serialize graph and weights, deserialize, execute the graph.
code.theory_link: TensorFlow Serving serves `tf.function` graphs with saved weights, the compilation mechanism of chapter 3.

parameters.name: "path/to/location"
parameters.role: Directory where the artifact is written and read from.

parameters.name: format="tf_saved_model"
parameters.role: Selects the TensorFlow SavedModel export format.

parameters.name: input_data
parameters.role: Batch of inputs for inference (placeholder name in the book).

pitfalls: Requires TensorFlow to be installed for export and reload, even if the model was trained with another backend.
Inputs must match the dtype and shape signature recorded at export time.
Any preprocessing done outside the model (e.g. normalization in NumPy) is not exported; apply the same preprocessing on the serving side or move it into the model.

code.title: Exporting to ONNX and running with ONNX Runtime
code.original_code:
model.export("path/to/location", format="onnx")

ort_session = onnxruntime.InferenceSession("path/to/location")
predictions = ort_session.run(None, input_data)
code.what_it_does: Exports the Keras model in ONNX format, loads it in an ONNX Runtime inference session, and runs it on input data.

line_explanations.explanation: Writes the model graph and weights in the framework-neutral ONNX format.
Creates an ONNX Runtime session that loads and prepares the model for execution.

`run(None, input_data)` executes the graph; `None` means return all outputs. In ONNX Runtime the inputs are normally given as a dict mapping input names to arrays, so `input_data` here stands for such a feed.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: trained Keras model; feed of input arrays. Output: ONNX file and a list of output arrays.
code.algorithm: Same export, load, execute flow as SavedModel, with a different format and runtime.
code.theory_link: ONNX also lifts weights and the graph out of Python, enabling serving from other environments.

parameters.name: None (first arg of run)
parameters.role: List of output names to fetch; None fetches all.

pitfalls: Requires the `onnxruntime` package (and ONNX export dependencies) to be installed and imported.
Input names and dtypes must match the exported graph (e.g. float32).
Not every custom layer or op converts to ONNX; test the exported model's outputs against the original.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written, illustrative: checking the ONNX export against the original model
import numpy as np, onnxruntime
sess = onnxruntime.InferenceSession("path/to/location")
name = sess.get_inputs()[0].name
x = np.random.rand(4, 784).astype("float32")   # example input shape
onnx_out = sess.run(None, {name: x})[0]
print(np.abs(onnx_out - model.predict(x)).max())  # should be ~1e-6

deeper.title: What 'lifting the graph out of Python' means
deeper.body:
Beyond the book:

1. During export, Keras runs the model's forward pass symbolically on placeholder inputs with known shapes and dtypes.
2. Each tensor operation is recorded as a node (matmul, add, relu, ...), producing a graph, as `tf.function` tracing did in chapter 3.
3. Current weight values are saved alongside as constants or variables.
4. A runtime written in C++ (TensorFlow Serving, ONNX Runtime) reads graph and weights and executes the nodes directly, with no Python interpreter involved.
5. A web server layer wraps this runtime and exposes an HTTP endpoint, completing the REST API.

deeper.title: REST checklist applied to example projects
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, applying the page's three conditions:

- **Fraud detection** (p.208): backend service, always online, a few hundred ms acceptable, data already on the company's servers, so REST is a good fit (p.210 agrees).
- **AR glasses object labeling:** needs responses in tens of ms, so it fails the latency condition; use on-device.
- **Private chat spam filter:** messages should not be decrypted on a server, so it fails the sensitivity condition; use on-device or in-browser (p.211 uses this example).

deeper.title: A restaurant kitchen
deeper.body: A REST API is like ordering from a central kitchen: you send your order (input) over the phone line (network), the kitchen (server) cooks it (inference) and delivers the result. It works if the phone line is up, you can wait for delivery, and you don't mind the kitchen seeing what you ordered.

misconceptions.claim: Serving a Keras model requires running Python on the server.
misconceptions.correction: TensorFlow Serving and ONNX lift the weights and computation graph outside Python, so they can be served from, e.g., a C++ server.

misconceptions.claim: SSL encryption makes it safe to send highly sensitive data to a model server.
misconceptions.correction: SSL protects data in transit, but the server must see the decrypted data to run the model; the page advises REST only when data is not highly sensitive.

misconceptions.claim: Export locks you into the TensorFlow backend for training.
misconceptions.correction: export() is available on all Keras models; Keras lets you train with one backend and use TensorFlow-ecosystem tooling for inference (p.115).
A typical round trip is around 500 ms, which is too slow when latency requirements are strict.

tf.function and graph mode, the compilation mechanism referenced here.
Keras backends; running inference with TensorFlow-ecosystem tooling.

later.note: Good fits for REST, managed cloud serving, and on-device deployment.
Deploying in the browser with TensorFlow.js or ONNX's JavaScript runtime.
Monitoring the model in the wild.

takeaways: Serving via a REST API is perhaps the easiest way to turn a model into a product.
Keras supports TensorFlow Serving and ONNX via model.export(); both lift weights and a computation graph out of Python.
TensorFlow Serving essentially serves tf.function graphs with saved weights, the compilation mechanism of chapter 3.
SavedModel: export with format="tf_saved_model", reload with tf.saved_model.load(...).serve(x). ONNX: format="onnx", onnxruntime.InferenceSession(...).run(None, x).
Use REST when there is reliable connectivity, latency needs are loose (about 500 ms round trip) and inputs are not highly sensitive; always use SSL.

questions.question: What do TensorFlow Serving and ONNX have in common, according to the page?
options: Both require the model to be written in TensorFlow
Both lift the model weights and a computation graph outside the Python program
Both run only in the browser
Both retrain the model on the server
questions.answer: Both lift the model weights and a computation graph outside the Python program
questions.explanation: That is how the page describes both. Any Keras model can be exported; neither is browser-only; and both serve inference artifacts, not training.

questions.question: Write the line that exports a Keras model for ONNX, and the line that creates the ONNX Runtime session.
questions.explanation: These are the first two statements of the ONNX snippet; predictions come from ort_session.run(None, input_data).

questions.question: Why does the page compare TensorFlow Serving to the compilation mechanism of chapter 3?
questions.answer: Because TensorFlow Serving serves tf.function computation graphs with a saved set of weights. Exporting traces the model into a static graph, as tf.function does, that can run without the original Python code.
questions.explanation: The page says 'If this sounds a lot like the compilation mechanism discussed in chapter 3 you are spot-on.'

questions.question: Which application is the worst fit for REST API deployment, based on the page's conditions?
options: A web search engine ranking images
A mobile app that must work in airplane mode
A music recommender on a website
questions.answer: A mobile app that must work in airplane mode
questions.explanation: The first condition is reliable internet access, and the page uses exactly the airplane-mode example. The other three are online, latency-tolerant services (p.210 lists several of them as good fits).

questions.question: What typical round-trip latency does the page give for REST serving, and what does that imply?
questions.answer: Around 500 ms; the setup is only suitable when the application does not have strict latency requirements.
questions.explanation: Request, inference and answer together typically take about half a second.

questions.question: If the request is SSL-encrypted, why does the page still say REST is unsuitable for highly sensitive data?
questions.answer: SSL protects data only in transit. On the server the data must be decrypted so the model can see it, exposing it to the server operator or attackers.
questions.explanation: The page states the data must be available on the server in decrypted form.

questions.question: For a model you have trained, decide whether you would export to SavedModel or ONNX and whether REST deployment fits. Justify with the page's three conditions.
questions.answer: Open-ended; a good answer checks connectivity, latency and data sensitivity and names a runtime suited to the target environment.
questions.explanation: Applying the checklist to a real case consolidates the decision criteria.
